meta.title: Topophany — self-hosted network monitoring in the terminal
meta.description: Self-hosted network monitoring in the terminal: a live map of your machines, paths and services, checked from the places you connect from, with the evidence behind every state. One Go binary.
meta.og-description: From where, via which path, reaching what — and on what evidence. Self-hosted network monitoring with a terminal UI, in one Go binary.
meta.image-alt: The Topophany globe in ink on paper, dithered like a print, above the pixel wordmark TOPOPHANY and its gloss, The appearance of a place.

hero.lede.html: From where, via which path, reaching what — and on what evidence.
hero.sub: Your whole network on one screen: which paths work from which places, which services answer, and the evidence behind every state. Self-hosted, one Go binary, read in the terminal.
hero.globe: A dithered globe in ink on paper, turning slowly: the globe of topophany-bar’s icon.

chapter.outage.title: An outage arrives
chapter.outage.text: Press x and home loses the line to the transit host in Los Angeles. Only confirmed failures turn red.
chapter.route.title: Follow the route
chapter.route.text: Select a problem and its route lights up. Enter shows the evidence.
chapter.vantage.title: Two vantage points
chapter.vantage.text: Down from Seattle, fine from New York. Each observer reports only what it can see.
chapter.virtual.title: Virtual geo
chapter.virtual.text: A schematic world that keeps the order of places, not their distances.
chapter.geo.title: Geo
chapter.geo.text: A braille world map. Nodes sit where you put them, not where an IP lookup guesses.
chapter.network.title: Network
chapter.network.text: Sources on the left, each link one column further right.
chapter.servers.title: Servers
chapter.servers.text: A card per server: its services, addresses, containers and your notes. s sets every card to one size; Enter lays one open.
chapter.incidents.title: Incidents
chapter.incidents.text: What failed, what other observers still see, and guesses labeled as guesses.
chapter.about.title: About
chapter.about.text: τόπος, place, and φαίνω, to bring to light.
demo.keys.html: 1–9 chapters space pause. Or run topo preview yourself.
evidence.title: Evidence, not colors
evidence.lead.html: Nothing turns green without a passing check. What nobody monitors stays unknown.
green.title: Nothing is green by default
green.site-edge: answered by Cloudflare FRA · cache DYNAMIC
green.text.html: Healthy rows stay quiet. No check means unknown, never up.
vantage.title: Vantage points are explicit
vantage.label: From Seattle the path to the server in Los Angeles times out; from New York it answers with HTTP 200. Verdict: a fault on Seattle's path, not a server outage.
vantage.verdict: fault on the path from Seattle · server up
vantage.text: A failure seen from one place is a fault on that path, not a server outage.
edge.title: The edge answered
edge.label: A check from Frankfurt asks for the site through Cloudflare. The edge cannot reach the origin in New York and answers HTTP 521 itself: the edge is up, and the origin is not proven either way.
edge.verdict: the fault lies behind the edge · origin unproven
edge.text: An answer from the CDN proves the edge, whatever it says. Only a check of its own proves the origin.
guess.title: A guess is labeled a guess
guess.label: An incident's evidence
guess.text: Incidents show their evidence. Anything more is marked as a hypothesis.
arch.title: One binary, three roles
arch.lead.html: topo is the client, the collector and the observer. No CGO, no database, no external modules.
arch.label: Workers at each vantage point send observations to two independent collectors, which the read-only TUI clients query.
notes.collectors-text: Workers send to both and buffer while one is away.
notes.readonly-text.html: No remote config API, no remote shell. Topology is local JSON you review.
notes.bounded-text: When a quota fills, probing stops with an error rather than dropping evidence.
probes.title: What it measures
probes.lead: Native probes, proxy chains, and read-only adapters for tools you already run.
probes.http: expected status, body, headers and egress IP
probes.ssh: an SSH banner, not a login
probes.tls: a verified certificate chain and name
probes.tcp: a connection, and nothing behind it
probes.chain-note: Up to 12 hops. HTTP, TCP, TLS and SSH checks run through every one, in order.
probes.mihomo: mode, chain and selection, as the core reports them
probes.wireguard: last handshake and byte counts; keys never kept
probes.cloudflared: tunnel sessions and their colos, as the connector reports them
probes.adapters-note: What a tool reports is shown as reported, never as an end-to-end pass.
probes.cloudflare: Workers and Pages; the POP that answered
probes.vercel: Functions; the edge and function region
probes.edges-note: An answer is credited to the edge that sent it, never to the origin behind it.
agent.title: Let your agent draw the map
agent.lead.html: Describing a network is the slow part of monitoring it, and the coding agent you already use is good at it. It reads what your machines already say about themselves, writes the topology, and checks it with topo validate before anything runs.
agent.prompt: Write a Topophany topology of my network to topology.json. Learn the format from `topo preview --print-topology` and docs/REFERENCE.md in github.com/WhitenWhiten/topophany. Read my SSH config, `tailscale status`, and the Compose files and reverse-proxy configs you can find. Declare each machine with where it is, the services on it, the applications they belong to and the addresses they answer on, add checks from the machines I will run workers on, and write what you learn about each machine into its notes. Never put a secret in the file. Run `topo validate --config topology.json` until it passes, then tell me what you found and what you guessed.
agent.ask-note: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor or any agent that can run commands. Secrets stay out: the format names environment variables and key files, never what is in them.
agent.memo-text: One reviewed file says what runs where and how each machine is reached, with notes and runbooks beside them. Your agent reads it before touching anything; you review its edits as a diff.
agent.quick-text: Text or JSON in one command, for you or your agent: is anything wrong, what runs on that server, how a check fared overnight.
agent.first-text: Preview draws your own network on synthetic evidence, so the two of you can look it over before a single worker starts.
duo.title: The map above the hinge
duo.lead.html: There's no iPhone app yet. What there is, is the TUI's design for one: --device lays the TUI out for the screen of an iPhone, an iPad, or iPhone Duo in each of its poses, and simulates that screen in your terminal. On the open Duo, what you look at and what you touch go on either side of the crease.
duo.alt: The TUI laid out for iPhone Duo held upright, as the terminal simulator draws it: the network map above the hinge, an affected route in amber; below it the status card reading 5 incidents, the observers, what needs attention, and the tabs along the foot
duo.caption.html: Drawn by the terminal simulator, upright and part folded like a laptop: topo preview --device duo-laptop.
duo.look-text: Laid out for the laptop pose, the map goes on the raised half, the screen, and the events and every control on the flat half, where fingers rest.
duo.bend-text: The layout keeps the crease clear even lying flat, so folding moves no cell. Fold, unfold or turn the simulated phone, and the tab, the selection and the open evidence stay put.
duo.clear-text: The layout puts no control on the crease, under the clock or the camera, or outside the safe area, and makes every target a finger tall. The tests check every tab on every device.
duo.try-note.html: [ and ] fold it through the poses, \ picks the next device, and the mouse stands in for a finger. The terminal needs about 99×70 cells. Until the next release, --device is on main.
duo.layouts: How each device is laid out
duo.poses-alt: The TUI laid out for iPhone Duo in five poses, as the terminal simulator draws them, the same moment in each: shut on the cover display with the tabs in the column under the clock, open sideways with the map on the left and the list on the right, part folded like a book, upright with the map above the hinge, and part folded like a laptop
duo.poses-caption: The same moment in every pose, as the simulator draws it. Shut, the tabs go in the column under the clock; open sideways, each side of the spread gets a job; upright, the map goes above the hinge.
bar.title: Your network in the menu bar
bar.lead.html: topophany-bar is Topophany’s macOS companion. It reads your collectors through topo: the status sits in the menu bar, a panel shows where a problem is seen, and desktop widgets keep servers and services in view.
bar.alt: A macOS desktop: the White Night icon in the menu bar, its moon in partial eclipse beside a count of 2; the panel open beneath it, showing a degraded network with two warnings, the observers that see them and a map; and Status, Server, Time Zones, Service and Map widgets on the desktop
bar.caption: A demo network with two warnings, rendered by the app’s own views from synthetic data.
bar.meta: macOS 26 or later · pre-release, built from source
bar.glance-text: The status as an icon, a count or a few words. In White Night, the built-in dithered sky, the moon is the status: full when all is clear, eclipsed while something is degraded, a blood moon while something is down.
bar.where-text: Incidents, the applications they touch and the observers reporting them, in one panel. Open any of them in the terminal UI for the evidence.
bar.direct-text: Pick servers from a Beszel Hub or a Komari server and watch their CPU, memory and disk, with no collector to run.
bar.widgets-text: Status, server, service, map and time-zone widgets, in six themes, from native macOS to the terminal UI printed on paper.
